reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that medical progress is not uniformly beneficial but exhibits a dual nature: it enhances diagnostic precision and treatment outcomes, yet simultaneously introduces biases and inefficiencies. Diagnostic expansion leads to inflated success rates by including less severe cases, creating a false impression of improved care. Therapeutic efficiency decays over time due to pathogen adaptation, necessitating evolving treatment paradigms. Selection bias in early mortality data distorts perceptions of disease lethality. These interrelated phenomena form a feedback loop where increased diagnostic capability can paradoxically obscure true therapeutic impact. The mathematical structure reveals a non-linear relationship between diagnostic thresholds and treatment efficacy, where marginal gains in early detection yield diminishing returns in overall health improvement. This creates a fundamental tension between the perceived progress and actual biological complexity.
